title: Hematologic complications in pregnancy
covers: Thrombocytopenia in pregnancy (gestational, ITP, preeclampsia/HELLP, AFLP, TTP, CM-HUS), anemia and iron deficiency, VTE and anticoagulants in pregnancy, thrombophilia prophylaxis, and postpartum hemorrhage.

items.p: Approach: timing of onset, degree of thrombocytopenia, other findings.

table: ITP, drug-induced, type IIB vWD, congenital
TTP, CM-HUS, SLE/APS, viral infection, marrow disorders, nutritional deficiency, splenic sequestration, thyroid disorders

ul: Overall: GT 76%, preeclampsia 20%, ITP 3%, other 1%. The differential varies by trimester and severity.

items.caption: Cause by trimester and platelet count

ul: 1st trimester: mostly ITP at any count. 2nd: GT above 100, ITP below 100. 3rd: GT above 100, preeclampsia below 50 (×10⁹/L).
Workup: CBC and smear, reticulocytes, coagulation screen, liver, thyroid and renal function, viral serologies.
Type IIB vWD or congenital thrombocytopenia: consider with a personal or family history of bleeding.

items.p: GT: smear shows fewer platelets, normal red and white cells; recheck labs in about 2 weeks.

table: Maternal: gestational diabetes, PPROM, hypertension, mood lability, insomnia. Fetal: cleft palate in early pregnancy
Rapid but short-lived response. Maternal: thrombosis, hemolysis

ul: Avoid dexamethasone: it crosses the placenta more easily. No ITP therapy is FDA-approved in pregnancy.

Second-line (little safety data): TPO receptor agonists (mostly romiplostim; refractory disease late in pregnancy), rituximab (slow, up to 8 weeks; maternal and neonatal immunosuppression), splenectomy (second trimester, laparoscopic, after vaccines). Others: azathioprine, dapsone, cyclosporine, anti-RhD immunoglobulin.
Contraindicated: danazol, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, vinca alkaloids.
Slide cases: 53 ×10⁹/L at 9 weeks, no bleeding → observe. 15 ×10⁹/L with bruising at 25 weeks → prednisone.
Preeclampsia: after 20 weeks, hypertension + proteinuria and/or end-organ dysfunction.
Severe features: severe hypertension, platelets < 100 ×10⁹/L, impaired liver function, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, CNS dysfunction. Can progress to a thrombotic microangiopathy.

HELLP: Hemolysis (MAHA), Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets. A preeclampsia variant; 15–20% occur without hypertension or proteinuria. After 20 weeks through early postpartum. RUQ pain, malaise, nausea, vomiting. Treatment: delivery.
Slide case: 31 weeks, BP 150/90, 3+ protein, platelets 45, Hb 9.3, LDH 588, haptoglobin < 5, AST/ALT ~ 220, schistocytes; normal bilirubin, PT, PTT, glucose, creatinine → HELLP.
Third trimester; rapid-onset liver failure.
Frequent coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, renal failure; mild-moderate thrombocytopenia with no or mild MAHA.
RUQ pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, headache, malaise, encephalopathy, jaundice. Treatment: delivery.
AFLP and HELLP look alike late in pregnancy: normal glucose, PT and bilirubin make AFLP less likely.

TTP: pregnancy is a trigger. Suspect when a TMA appears before 20 weeks with platelets < 30, especially with neurologic or cardiac findings and normal BP. Confirm with ADAMTS13 < 10%; no antibody → congenital TTP. Treat with plasma exchange + corticosteroids (plasma infusions if congenital). Caplacizumab: safety in pregnancy unknown.
CM-HUS: pregnancy amplifies complement. Suspect with severe AKI or a new/worsening TMA postpartum. Treat with eculizumab.

items.caption: Typical pregnancy-specific TMA: manage, then reassess at 48–72 h postpartum

ul: Atypical features (severe neurologic or cardiac findings, severe AKI, new/worsening TMA postpartum, onset before 20 weeks, severe thrombocytopenia) → send ADAMTS13 and consider plasma exchange while awaiting it. ADAMTS13 < 10% → TTP; otherwise severe AKI → CM-HUS.
Anemia (ACOG, CDC): Hb < 11 g/dL in the 1st and 3rd trimesters, < 10.5 g/dL in the 2nd.
Physiologic anemia: plasma volume rises relative to red cell mass.
Iron deficiency outcomes. Maternal: fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, preterm labor, more transfusions. Fetal: low birth weight, long-term neurocognitive effects, reduced iron stores.
Non-anemic iron deficiency comes first; iron deficiency anemia is the extreme end.
Ferritin 12 ng/mL: only 25% sensitive. Ferritin 30 ng/mL: 92% sensitive, 98% specific. ASH: in anemic pregnant patients, ferritin ≤ 50 ng/mL may be used.
Treatment: oral iron early in pregnancy or for mild deficiency; IV iron in the 2nd or 3rd trimester.

Risk factors: heavy menstrual bleeding, teenage pregnancy, hyperemesis gravidarum, multiple gestation, vaginal bleeding after the 1st trimester, abnormal placentation, interpregnancy interval < 18 months, multiparity.

table: Gravid uterus compressing veins, vein dilation, immobilization
↓ protein S, ↓ fibrinolysis; ↑ VWF, factor VIII, fibrinogen; ↑ D-dimer; protein C and antithrombin unchanged
Do not cross the placenta; no routine anti-Xa monitoring of LMWH
Teratogen; antepartum only for prosthetic heart valves
Likely cross the placenta and enter breast milk

ul: Slide case: PE at 15 weeks → enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily. On therapeutic LMWH and wanting an epidural → scheduled delivery with LMWH stopped 24 hours before.

items.p: Slide case: homozygous FVL with affected sister and mother → antepartum and postpartum prophylaxis.

items.note: The slide's table carries asterisks that are not explained on the slide. Duration of anticoagulation after a PE in pregnancy is asked on slide 47 but not answered; it was not tested.

ul: ACOG: > 1000 mL blood loss, or blood loss with signs of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of delivery. A leading cause of maternal death worldwide.
Causes: tone (uterine atony), trauma (laceration, uterine rupture), tissue (retained placenta), thrombin (coagulopathy).
Management: uterotonics, obstetric interventions (massage, packing, balloon tamponade, surgery, interventional radiology), transfusion, antifibrinolytics. Tranexamic acid reduces death from bleeding.

items.note: The slide says "> 1000 cc"; ACOG's wording is "≥ 1000 mL". The exact boundary was not tested.

cards.q: Most common cause of thrombocytopenia in pregnancy
cards.a: Gestational thrombocytopenia (76%); then preeclampsia (20%), ITP (3%)
1st: ITP. 2nd: GT above 100, ITP below 100. 3rd: GT above 100, preeclampsia below 50 (×10⁹/L).
Late onset (late 2nd/early 3rd trimester), usually > 70 ×10⁹/L, not outside pregnancy, no neonatal thrombocytopenia, resolves postpartum
ITP: any time, mild to severe, can exist outside pregnancy, can cause neonatal thrombocytopenia

cards.q: Isolated thrombocytopenia with a bleeding history: what else to consider?
cards.a: Type IIB vWD and congenital thrombocytopenia
Treat if < 20–30 in the first 8 months; > 50 for delivery; > 70 for epidural (×10⁹/L)
Prednisone or IVIG (avoid dexamethasone: crosses the placenta more easily)
Maternal: gestational diabetes, PPROM, hypertension, mood, insomnia. Fetal: cleft palate (early)
Rapid but short-lived response; maternal thrombosis and hemolysis
TPO-RA (refractory, late pregnancy), rituximab (slow, up to 8 weeks), splenectomy (2nd trimester)
Danazol, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, vinca alkaloids
Preeclampsia + severe HTN, platelets < 100, liver impairment, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema or CNS dysfunction
Hemolysis (MAHA), elevated liver enzymes, low platelets; after 20 weeks to early postpartum; 15–20% without HTN/proteinuria; delivery
3rd trimester; rapid liver failure, coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, renal failure, encephalopathy; little MAHA; delivery
Normal glucose, PT and bilirubin make AFLP less likely

cards.q: When to suspect TTP in pregnancy
cards.a: TMA before 20 weeks, platelets < 30, neurologic/cardiac findings, normal BP

cards.q: TTP in pregnancy: confirm and treat
cards.a: ADAMTS13 < 10%; plasma exchange + steroids (plasma infusions if congenital); caplacizumab safety unknown
Mostly postpartum; severe AKI; creatinine worsens after delivery; eculizumab
Severe AKI → CM-HUS (eculizumab); otherwise work up TTP (ADAMTS13)
Hb < 11 g/dL in 1st and 3rd trimesters; < 10.5 g/dL in 2nd
Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass

cards.q: Iron in pregnancy: oral or IV?
cards.a: Oral early or if mild; IV in the 2nd or 3rd trimester
12: only 25% sensitive. 30: 92% sensitive, 98% specific. ASH: ≤ 50 in anemic patients
↓ protein S, ↓ fibrinolysis; ↑ VWF, VIII, fibrinogen, D-dimer; protein C and antithrombin unchanged
LMWH/UFH: yes. Fondaparinux: HIT or heparin allergy. Warfarin: no (except prosthetic valves). DOACs: no.
LMWH, UFH, fondaparinux, warfarin: yes. Xa inhibitors and oral DTIs: avoid.
Scheduled delivery; stop LMWH 24 hours before

cards.q: Thrombophilias needing antepartum and postpartum prophylaxis
cards.a: Homozygous FVL, combined thrombophilia, antithrombin deficiency with family history
Protein C or S deficiency with family history; homozygous prothrombin mutation without family history
Tone (atony), trauma (laceration, rupture), tissue (retained placenta), thrombin (coagulopathy)

cards.q: Drug that reduces bleeding deaths in PPH
cards.a: Tranexamic acid

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 33 weeks has a platelet count of 110 ×10⁹/L, down from 165 ×10⁹/L in the first trimester. She is normotensive with normal Hb, WBC, coagulation tests and liver enzymes. The smear shows fewer platelets with normal red and white cells. She had low platelets in her last pregnancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Isolated, mild, late-onset thrombocytopenia with a normal smear in a well woman is gestational thrombocytopenia, the commonest cause (76%). GT is typically late 2nd or early 3rd trimester and usually > 70 ×10⁹/L. A: Possible, but late onset and mild degree favor GT. C: She is normotensive. D: Needs hemolysis and raised liver enzymes. E: Considered with a bleeding history.

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks is diagnosed with gestational thrombocytopenia (platelets 105 ×10⁹/L, normal smear, normal blood pressure and liver tests). What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Case 1: she is thought to have GT, with a plan to recheck labs in 2 weeks. GT is mild and resolves postpartum. A: Treatment is for ITP below 20–30 ×10⁹/L. B: Not needed for GT. D: Not part of the workup. E: GT does not change the delivery plan.

questions.stem: A woman has a platelet count of 95 ×10⁹/L at 36 weeks. A CBC two years before pregnancy showed 98 ×10⁹/L. Which diagnosis does this history argue against?
questions.explanation: Gestational thrombocytopenia does not occur outside pregnancy. ITP may. A: Can be present outside pregnancy. B: Inherited; present before pregnancy. C: Lifelong. E: Can lower platelets at any time.

questions.stem: Gestational thrombocytopenia usually keeps the platelet count above what level?
questions.explanation: GT is mild: usually > 70 ×10⁹/L. B: ITP treatment range. C: TTP clue below this. D: Delivery target in ITP. E: Too high; GT is a fall below normal.

questions.stem: A woman had thrombocytopenia throughout pregnancy, and her newborn also has a low platelet count. Which maternal disorder best explains both?
questions.explanation: ITP: neonatal thrombocytopenia is possible. GT: no neonatal thrombocytopenia. A: No neonatal thrombocytopenia. B: Affects only the mother's count. C: Maternal production defect. D: Not a platelet disorder.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of thrombocytopenia in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: GT 76%, preeclampsia 20%, ITP 3%, other 1%. The differential varies by trimester and severity. A: About 20%. C: About 3%. D: Part of the preeclampsia spectrum. E: Rare.

questions.stem: In a pregnant woman with isolated thrombocytopenia, which finding most favors immune thrombocytopenia over gestational thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: Approach: timing of onset, degree, other findings. ITP dominates the first trimester and can be severe; GT is late onset and mild. A: Mild; fits GT. B: Both. D: Both. E: Both.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old at 9 weeks has a platelet count of 53 ×10⁹/L. She has no bleeding history. Hb, WBC, liver tests, PT and PTT are normal; HIV and HCV are negative; the smear shows fewer platelets with normal red and white cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Early (first-trimester) isolated thrombocytopenia below 70 ×10⁹/L with no bleeding history: ITP. GT is struck out by timing (late 2nd/early 3rd trimester). B: Late onset and usually > 70. C: After 20 weeks. D: After 20 weeks; hemolysis. E: Third trimester.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old at 9 weeks has ITP with a platelet count of 53 ×10⁹/L and no bleeding. What is the best management now?
questions.explanation: In the first 8 months, treat ITP if platelets < 20–30 ×10⁹/L. At 53 and asymptomatic, the platelet count is closely observed. A: Treat if < 20–30 ×10⁹/L. B: Not needed at this count. C: Avoided in pregnancy. D: Second-line.

questions.stem: A woman with ITP at 25 weeks now has a platelet count of 15 ×10⁹/L and easy bruising. Creatinine, liver tests, PT, PTT and fibrinogen are normal. What is the best treatment?
questions.explanation: Platelets < 20–30 ×10⁹/L in the first 8 months → treat. First-line: prednisone (0.25–1 mg/kg) or IVIG. A: Second-line; little data. B: Second-line; slow response. C: Count is below 20–30. E: Crosses the placenta more easily.

questions.stem: During the first 8 months of pregnancy, ITP is treated when the platelet count falls below what level?
questions.explanation: Treat ITP if platelets < 20–30 ×10⁹/L during the first 8 months. Near delivery: > 50 for labor and delivery, > 70 for epidural. A: Target for labor and delivery. B: Target for epidural. D: Severe preeclampsia cut-off. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A woman with ITP at 37 weeks wants an epidural for labor. Her platelet count should be above what level?
questions.explanation: Approaching delivery: > 50 ×10⁹/L for labor and delivery, > 70 ×10⁹/L for epidural. A: Enough for delivery, not epidural. B: Treatment threshold. C: Higher than needed. E: Lower limit of normal.

questions.stem: In a woman with ITP, what platelet count is targeted for labor and delivery?
questions.explanation: Approaching delivery: > 50 ×10⁹/L for labor and delivery, > 70 ×10⁹/L for epidural. B: Epidural target. C: Early-pregnancy treatment threshold. D: Higher than needed. E: Normal range.

questions.stem: A woman with ITP is started on prednisone at 26 weeks. Which maternal complication should be watched for?
questions.explanation: Prednisone, maternal: gestational diabetes, PPROM, hypertension, mood lability, insomnia. Fetal: cleft palate in early pregnancy. A: IVIG. B: IVIG. C: Rituximab. D: Fetal risk in early pregnancy.

questions.stem: A woman with ITP needs prednisone at 8 weeks. Which fetal risk applies at this stage?

options.D: Low birth weight from the drug

questions.explanation: Prednisone carries a fetal risk of cleft palate in early pregnancy. Maternal risks: gestational diabetes, PPROM, hypertension, mood lability, insomnia. A: Rituximab. C: Not a listed effect. D: Linked to iron deficiency. E: Not a listed effect.

questions.stem: A woman with ITP at 36 weeks has a platelet count of 22 ×10⁹/L and needs a fast rise before delivery. Which first-line therapy gives a rapid but short-lived response?
questions.explanation: IVIG (0.4–2 g/kg in divided doses over 1–5 days): rapid but short-lived response; maternal thrombotic risk and hemolysis. A: First-line, but not the rapid short-lived one. B: Response takes up to 8 weeks. C: Second-line, for refractory disease. D: Second trimester.

questions.stem: Which maternal adverse effect is linked to IVIG given for ITP in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: IVIG, maternal: thrombotic risk and hemolysis. Prednisone, maternal: gestational diabetes, PPROM, hypertension, mood lability, insomnia. A: Prednisone. C: Prednisone. D: Prednisone. E: Rituximab.

questions.stem: A resident suggests dexamethasone for a pregnant woman with ITP. Why is prednisone used instead?

options.A: Dexamethasone crosses the placenta more easily
options.B: Dexamethasone acts too slowly on platelets
options.D: Dexamethasone carries a higher thrombotic risk
options.E: Prednisone has no known effects on the fetus

questions.explanation: Avoid dexamethasone: it crosses the placenta more easily, with adverse fetal effects. There are no FDA-approved ITP therapies in pregnancy. B: Not the reason. C: No ITP therapy is FDA-approved in pregnancy. D: That is IVIG. E: It carries a cleft palate risk.

questions.stem: Which ITP therapy in pregnancy works slowly (up to 8 weeks) and risks maternal and neonatal immunosuppression?
questions.explanation: Rituximab: slow response (up to 8 weeks), risk of maternal and neonatal immunosuppression and infection. A: TPO receptor agonist. B: Rapid response. D: First-line. E: Surgical.

questions.stem: A woman at 35 weeks has ITP that has not responded to prednisone or IVIG. Her platelet count is 12 ×10⁹/L. Which drug class is reserved for this situation?
questions.explanation: TPO receptor agonists (most reports with romiplostim) are reserved for refractory disease late in pregnancy. A: Rituximab responds too slowly (up to 8 weeks). B: Contraindicated. C: Cyclophosphamide is contraindicated. E: Dexamethasone crosses the placenta.

questions.stem: If a pregnant woman with refractory ITP needs splenectomy, when is it best done?
questions.explanation: Splenectomy can be performed in the second trimester, laparoscopically, after vaccines. A: Not the recommended time. C: Not the recommended time. D: Not the recommended time. E: Not a pregnancy option.

questions.stem: Which drug is contraindicated for ITP in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Contraindicated: danazol, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, vinca alkaloids. Others (little data): azathioprine, dapsone, cyclosporine, anti-RhD immunoglobulin. B: Listed with other second-line options. C: Listed with other second-line options. D: Listed with other second-line options. E: Listed with other second-line options.

questions.stem: Each can be considered for refractory ITP in pregnancy EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Contraindicated: danazol, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide and vinca alkaloids. A: Refractory disease late in pregnancy. B: Second-line; slow. C: Other option; little data. D: Other option; little data.

questions.stem: A woman at 12 weeks has a platelet count of 85 ×10⁹/L and nothing else abnormal. She and her mother have had heavy periods and nosebleeds all their lives. Besides ITP, which diagnosis must be considered?
questions.explanation: Type IIB vWD and congenital thrombocytopenia are considered when isolated thrombocytopenia comes with a personal or family history of bleeding. A: Late onset. B: After 20 weeks; other findings. D: Other findings (MAHA). E: Third trimester.

questions.stem: Which test belongs to the recommended workup of thrombocytopenia in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Recommended: CBC and smear, reticulocyte count, coagulation screen, liver, thyroid and renal function, viral serologies. A: Not listed. B: Not listed. C: Fanconi anemia. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: At 36 weeks, a woman is found to have a platelet count of 40 ×10⁹/L. Before any other result is known, which cause is most likely?
questions.explanation: Third trimester: above 100 ×10⁹/L mostly GT; below 50 ×10⁹/L mostly preeclampsia. B: Mild; dominates above 100. C: A smaller share in the third trimester. D: Small share. E: Small share.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old at 31 weeks has 2 days of RUQ pain, headache and vomiting. BP 150/90 mmHg; urine protein 3+. Platelets 45 ×10⁹/L (160 a month ago), Hb 9.3 g/dL, LDH 588 U/L, haptoglobin < 5 mg/dL, AST 219 U/L, ALT 216 U/L, bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, PT and PTT normal, glucose 103 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. The smear shows schistocytes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hemolysis (MAHA: low Hb, high LDH, low haptoglobin, schistocytes), elevated liver enzymes and low platelets after 20 weeks with hypertension and proteinuria = HELLP. A: Normal glucose, PT and bilirubin. B: Hypertension and liver injury favor HELLP. C: Creatinine is normal. E: No hemolysis in ITP.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks has hypertension, RUQ pain, schistocytes, high LDH, AST 240 U/L and platelets 50 ×10⁹/L. Glucose, PT and bilirubin are normal. What is the mainstay of treatment?
questions.explanation: HELLP: mainstay of treatment is delivery, with symptomatic management and close monitoring. A: TTP. B: CM-HUS. D: ITP. E: ITP.

questions.stem: A woman at 35 weeks has RUQ pain, nausea, AST 310 U/L and a platelet count of 70 ×10⁹/L. Which result argues most against acute fatty liver of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: AFLP and HELLP have similar features and present late; normal glucose, PT and bilirubin make AFLP less likely. A: AFLP has frequent coagulopathy. B: AFLP causes jaundice. C: AFLP causes renal failure. D: AFLP has mild-moderate thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A woman at 36 weeks has nausea, vomiting, anorexia, jaundice and confusion. Glucose 45 mg/dL, PT prolonged, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, AST 280 U/L, platelets 95 ×10⁹/L; the smear shows few schistocytes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: AFLP: third trimester, rapid-onset liver failure, frequent coagulopathy, hypoglycemia and renal failure; mild-moderate thrombocytopenia with no or mild MAHA; encephalopathy and jaundice. A: Hypoglycemia, coagulopathy and encephalopathy point to AFLP. C: Liver failure is not typical. D: Liver failure is not typical. E: Isolated thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: Which feature characterizes acute fatty liver of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: AFLP is characterized by rapid-onset liver failure, with frequent coagulopathy, hypoglycemia and renal failure. A: CM-HUS. B: TTP. C: HELLP; AFLP has no or mild MAHA. D: Gestational thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: Preeclampsia requires new hypertension after what gestational age?
questions.explanation: Preeclampsia: > 20 weeks with hypertension + proteinuria and/or end-organ dysfunction. A: Too early. B: Too late. D: Too late. E: Too late.

questions.stem: A woman at 33 weeks has a BP of 148/92 mmHg and 2+ proteinuria. Which additional finding makes this preeclampsia with severe features?
questions.explanation: Severe if severe organ manifestations, including platelets < 100 ×10⁹/L (also severe hypertension, impaired liver function, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, CNS dysfunction). A: Above 100. B: Not a severe feature. C: Not a severe feature. E: Not a severe feature.

questions.stem: Which finding is a severe feature of preeclampsia?
questions.explanation: Preeclampsia + one of: severe hypertension, low platelets, impaired liver function, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, CNS dysfunction. B: Not severe. C: Above 100. D: Not severe. E: Normal.

questions.stem: At 34 weeks, a normotensive woman without proteinuria has RUQ pain, schistocytes, high LDH, AST 250 U/L and platelets 60 ×10⁹/L. Glucose, PT and bilirubin are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: 15–20% of HELLP cases occur without hypertension or proteinuria. Hemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets = HELLP. A: Normal glucose, PT and bilirubin. C: Needs hypertension. D: No hemolysis or liver injury. E: No hemolysis.

questions.stem: What share of HELLP cases occur without hypertension or proteinuria?
questions.explanation: HELLP is a variant of preeclampsia; 15–20% occur without hypertension or proteinuria. A: Too low. B: Too low. C: Too high. E: Too high.

questions.stem: In which period does HELLP syndrome occur?
questions.explanation: HELLP occurs after 20 weeks through early postpartum (< 72 h). B: TTP. C: CM-HUS. D: AFLP. E: Points to TTP.

questions.stem: Which thrombotic microangiopathy of pregnancy overlaps with preeclampsia with severe features?
questions.explanation: HELLP sits in both circles: preeclampsia with severe features and the TMAs (with TTP, CM-HUS and AFLP). A: Separate TMA. C: Separate TMA. D: Separate TMA. E: Not a TMA.

questions.stem: A woman at 14 weeks has confusion, normal blood pressure, platelets 18 ×10⁹/L, schistocytes, high LDH and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Liver enzymes are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TTP: consider if a TMA appears before 20 weeks with platelets < 30 ×10⁹/L, especially with severe neurologic or cardiac findings and normal blood pressure. Pregnancy is a known trigger. A: After 20 weeks. B: After 20 weeks; hypertension. D: Third trimester; liver failure. E: Severe AKI; mostly postpartum.

questions.stem: Which result confirms TTP in a pregnant woman with a thrombotic microangiopathy?
questions.explanation: TTP is confirmed with ADAMTS13 < 10%. Consider congenital TTP if the antibody is absent. A: CM-HUS. B: Severe preeclampsia. C: HELLP. D: AFLP.

questions.stem: A woman at 16 weeks has a thrombotic microangiopathy with platelets 15 ×10⁹/L, severe headache and normal blood pressure. ADAMTS13 has been sent; the result will take 3 days. What should be done now?
questions.explanation: Atypical presentation (before 20 weeks, severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic findings) → send ADAMTS13 and consider starting plasma exchange while awaiting the result. B: Plasma exchange is started while awaiting ADAMTS13. C: CM-HUS. D: Management of PEC/HELLP. E: ITP.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman has TTP with ADAMTS13 activity of 3% and no inhibitor antibody. What treatment fits?
questions.explanation: Absent antibody suggests congenital TTP, treated with plasma infusions. Acquired TTP: plasma exchange and corticosteroids. A: For acquired (antibody) TTP. B: Safety in pregnancy unknown. C: CM-HUS. D: PEC/HELLP.

questions.stem: Which TTP drug has unknown safety in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: TTP: plasma exchange and corticosteroids (plasma infusions in congenital TTP). The safety of caplacizumab in pregnancy is unknown. A: Used with plasma exchange. C: Corticosteroids are used. D: Plasma is used. E: CM-HUS treatment.

questions.stem: Two days after delivery for preeclampsia, a woman has ongoing hemolysis, platelets 50 ×10⁹/L and a creatinine that has risen from 0.8 to 4.2 mg/dL. ADAMTS13 activity is 35%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Consider CM-HUS with severe AKI or a new or worsening TMA postpartum. It is most common postpartum; delivery worsens creatinine. A: Should improve within 72 h postpartum. B: ADAMTS13 is above 10%. C: Liver failure. E: Should improve after delivery.

questions.stem: A woman has complement-mediated HUS 3 days after delivery, with severe AKI. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: CM-HUS is treated with eculizumab. A: TTP. B: Already delivered; not the treatment. D: ITP. E: ITP second-line.

questions.stem: Why can pregnancy trigger complement-mediated HUS?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is complement amplifying and may trigger CM-HUS, most commonly postpartum. B: TTP mechanism. C: AFLP. D: ITP. E: Physiologic anemia.

questions.stem: A woman with HELLP syndrome delivers at 32 weeks. At 72 hours postpartum, her platelet count and LDH have not improved; creatinine is normal. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: No improvement 48–72 h postpartum and no severe AKI → work up other TMAs, including TTP (ADAMTS13). A: Needs severe AKI. B: HELLP should improve within 48–72 h. C: ITP. E: ITP.

questions.stem: After delivery for preeclampsia or HELLP, the thrombotic microangiopathy should improve within what time?
questions.explanation: PEC/HELLP: improvement 48–72 h postpartum (resolution within 72 h). No improvement → consider CM-HUS or TTP. A: Too short. B: Too long. C: Too long. D: Too long.

questions.stem: A woman at 30 weeks has hypertension, proteinuria, schistocytes and platelets 60 ×10⁹/L. Which additional finding makes this atypical for a pregnancy-specific TMA and calls for an ADAMTS13 level?
questions.explanation: Atypical features: severe neurologic findings, cardiac findings, severe AKI, new or worsening TMA postpartum, presentation before 20 weeks, severe thrombocytopenia → send ADAMTS13. A: Typical of HELLP. C: Typical of HELLP. D: Typical of preeclampsia. E: Typical of HELLP.

questions.stem: Which pregnancy-associated TMA typically shows worsening kidney function after delivery?
questions.explanation: Effect of delivery: PE-SF/HELLP resolves within 72 h; TTP does not improve; CM-HUS shows worsening creatinine. A: Resolves within 72 h postpartum. B: Resolves within 72 h postpartum. D: No improvement; neurologic or cardiac findings. E: Delivery is the treatment.

questions.stem: In the second trimester, anemia is defined by a hemoglobin below what value?
questions.explanation: ACOG and CDC: Hb < 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, < 10.5 g/dL in the second. B: First and third trimesters. C: Non-pregnant women. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: Which pregnant woman meets the definition of anemia?
questions.explanation: Anemia: Hb < 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, < 10.5 g/dL in the second. A: Second-trimester cut-off is 10.5. B: Above 11. C: Above 11. D: Second-trimester cut-off is 10.5.

questions.stem: What causes physiologic anemia of pregnancy?

options.A: Red cell mass falls as erythropoiesis slows
options.B: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass
options.C: Iron is diverted from mother to fetus

questions.explanation: Physiologic anemia of pregnancy is due to increasing plasma volume relative to red cell mass. A: Not the mechanism. C: Iron deficiency. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which history most raises a pregnant woman's risk of iron deficiency?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy-specific risk factors: heavy menstrual bleeding history, teenage pregnancy, hyperemesis gravidarum, multiple gestation, vaginal bleeding after the first trimester, abnormal placentation, interpregnancy interval < 18 months, multiparity. A: Teenage pregnancy is the risk. B: Multiparity is the risk. C: Multiple gestation is the risk. E: Bleeding after the first trimester is the risk.

questions.stem: Maternal iron deficiency is linked to which fetal outcome?
questions.explanation: Fetal: low birth weight, long-term neurocognitive effects, reduced iron stores. Maternal: fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, preterm labor, increased transfusion rates. A: ITP. B: Prednisone. D: Rituximab. E: Not linked.

questions.stem: Maternal iron deficiency in pregnancy is linked to which maternal outcome?
questions.explanation: Maternal: fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, preterm labor and increased transfusion rates. A: Prednisone. B: IVIG. C: Prednisone. E: Prednisone.

questions.stem: At 30 weeks, a woman has Hb 9.0 g/dL and ferritin 8 ng/mL. Which treatment is preferred?
questions.explanation: Management: oral iron if early in pregnancy or mild deficiency; intravenous iron in the 2nd or 3rd trimester. B: Early pregnancy or mild deficiency. C: Not first-line for iron deficiency. D: Not indicated. E: Not the deficiency.

questions.stem: At 9 weeks, a woman has Hb 11.3 g/dL and ferritin 22 ng/mL. Which treatment is preferred?
questions.explanation: Non-anemic (early) iron deficiency early in pregnancy: oral iron. IV iron in the 2nd or 3rd trimester. A: 2nd or 3rd trimester. C: Not indicated. D: Not indicated. E: Iron deficiency has poor outcomes.

questions.stem: In pregnancy, a ferritin threshold of 30 ng/mL detects iron deficiency with about what sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Ferritin 12 ng/mL: only 25% sensitive. Ferritin 30 ng/mL: 92% sensitivity, 98% specificity. A: Threshold of 12 ng/mL. B: Not the value. D: Not the value. E: That is its specificity.

questions.stem: For a pregnant patient with anemia, which serum ferritin threshold may be used to diagnose iron deficiency?
questions.explanation: ASH: for pregnant individuals with anemia, a serum ferritin threshold of ≤ 50 ng/mL may be appropriate to diagnose iron deficiency. A: Only 25% sensitive. B: Too low. C: Too high. D: Too high.

questions.stem: How does non-anemic iron deficiency relate to iron deficiency anemia?

options.B: The most severe stage of deficiency
options.D: An earlier stage of iron depletion

questions.explanation: Non-anemic iron deficiency occurs in the early stages of iron depletion; iron deficiency anemia is the extreme end of the spectrum. A: Same spectrum. B: IDA is the extreme end. C: Physiologic anemia. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: Which coagulation change occurs in normal pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Hypercoagulable blood in pregnancy: protein S and fibrinolysis fall; VWF, factor VIII and fibrinogen rise; D-dimer rises; protein C and antithrombin are unchanged. B: Unchanged. C: Unchanged. D: Rises. E: Rises.

questions.stem: Which laboratory change is expected in a healthy pregnancy?
questions.explanation: D-dimer is increased in pregnancy; VWF, factor VIII and fibrinogen rise; protein S and fibrinolysis fall; protein C and antithrombin are unchanged. A: Unchanged. B: Decreased. D: Raised. E: Falls.

questions.stem: Which contributes to venous stasis in pregnancy?

options.A: Damage to pelvic vessels at delivery
options.B: Compression of veins by the gravid uterus

questions.explanation: Venous stasis: gravid uterus compressing vessels, vein dilation, immobilization. Vascular damage: pelvic vessels at delivery. A: Vascular damage. C: Hypercoagulability. D: Hypercoagulability. E: Hypercoagulability.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 15 weeks has dyspnea and pleuritic pain. CT pulmonary angiography shows segmental pulmonary emboli. Kidney and liver function are normal. Which anticoagulant should be started?
questions.explanation: Case 4: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily. LMWH and UFH do not cross the placenta and are safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding. A: Teratogen. B: Likely crosses the placenta. C: Likely crosses the placenta. D: Limited to HIT or heparin allergy.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia needs anticoagulation for DVT. Which drug fits?
questions.explanation: Fondaparinux: limited safety data in pregnancy; use limited to HIT or heparin allergy. A: Heparin causes HIT. C: Heparin product. D: Teratogen. E: Likely crosses the placenta.

questions.stem: Antepartum warfarin may still be used for which indication?
questions.explanation: Warfarin is a teratogen; antepartum use is not recommended for VTE. Exception: prosthetic heart valves. A: Not recommended for VTE. B: Not recommended for VTE. C: Prophylaxis uses heparins. E: Fondaparinux.

questions.stem: Which anticoagulant should be avoided in a breastfeeding mother?
questions.explanation: Xa inhibitors and oral DTIs likely cross the placenta and are present in breast milk: avoid. Warfarin, LMWH, UFH and fondaparinux are compatible with breastfeeding. A: Compatible with breastfeeding. B: Compatible. D: Compatible. E: Compatible.

questions.stem: For a pregnant woman on therapeutic LMWH, what is advised about anti-Xa levels?
questions.explanation: For LMWH, the guideline recommends against routine monitoring of anti-FXa levels. A: Not recommended. B: Not recommended. C: Not recommended. D: Not recommended.

questions.stem: A woman on enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily since a PE at 15 weeks is now 34 weeks. She wants a vaginal delivery with epidural anesthesia. What is the best plan?

options.A: Scheduled delivery with LMWH stopped 24 hours before
options.B: Spontaneous labor with LMWH stopped at its onset
options.C: Stopping LMWH now since 3 months have passed
options.D: Scheduled cesarean with LMWH stopped 24 hours before

questions.explanation: Case 4: scheduled delivery with discontinuation of LMWH 24 hours before, so that epidural anesthesia can be given. B: Epidural would be unsafe on full-dose LMWH. C: She still needs anticoagulation. D: No indication for cesarean. E: Teratogen; not for VTE.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 13 weeks has homozygous factor V Leiden. Her sister had a postpartum DVT and her mother an unprovoked PE. She has never had a thrombosis. What is recommended?
questions.explanation: Case 5: homozygous FVL → antepartum and postpartum anticoagulant prophylaxis. Antithrombin deficiency with family history and combined thrombophilia also get both. A: For heterozygous FVL. B: For established VTE. C: Not for VTE in pregnancy. E: Avoided in pregnancy.

questions.stem: Each woman below is pregnant, has no personal VTE and has a first-degree relative with VTE. Which one should receive antepartum and postpartum prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin deficiency: no prophylaxis without family history; antepartum and postpartum prophylaxis with family history. A: Postpartum prophylaxis. C: Postpartum prophylaxis. D: No prophylaxis. E: No prophylaxis.

questions.stem: Each woman below is pregnant, has no personal VTE and has a first-degree relative with VTE. Which one should receive postpartum, but not antepartum, prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Protein C or S deficiency: no prophylaxis without family history; postpartum prophylaxis with family history. A: No prophylaxis. B: Antepartum and postpartum. C: Antepartum and postpartum. D: No prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 13 weeks has heterozygous factor V Leiden. Her sister had a postpartum DVT. She has never had a thrombosis. What is recommended?

options.A: Prophylactic LMWH through pregnancy and puerperium

questions.explanation: FVL heterozygous or prothrombin gene heterozygous: no antepartum or postpartum prophylaxis. A: For homozygous FVL. B: For established VTE. D: Not for VTE in pregnancy. E: Avoided in pregnancy.

questions.stem: Each woman below is pregnant and has no personal or family history of VTE. Which one should receive postpartum prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Homozygous prothrombin gene mutation without family history: postpartum prophylaxis, no antepartum prophylaxis. B: No prophylaxis without family history. C: No prophylaxis without family history. D: No prophylaxis without family history. E: No prophylaxis.

questions.stem: Each woman below is pregnant and has no personal or family history of VTE. Which one should receive antepartum prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Combined thrombophilia and homozygous FVL: antepartum and postpartum prophylaxis regardless of family history. A: Postpartum prophylaxis. B: Needs a family history. C: Needs a family history. D: No prophylaxis.

questions.stem: Soon after a vaginal delivery, a woman loses 1.5 L of blood. The uterus is soft and boggy, the placenta was delivered complete and there are no tears. What is the cause of bleeding?
questions.explanation: Causes of PPH: tone (uterine atony), trauma (laceration, uterine rupture), tissue (retained placenta), thrombin (coagulopathies). A: Placenta was complete. B: No tears. C: Trauma; not suggested. E: Thrombin; uterus would be firm.

questions.stem: After delivery, a woman with HELLP syndrome bleeds from the uterus and from venipuncture sites. The uterus is firm, the placenta is complete and there are no tears. What is the cause of bleeding?
questions.explanation: PPH from thrombin (coagulopathies): bleeding from several sites with a firm uterus and no retained tissue or trauma. A: Uterus is firm. C: Placenta is complete. D: No tears. E: Not suggested.

questions.stem: Which drug reduces death from bleeding in postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: PPH management: uterotonics, obstetric interventions, transfusion, antifibrinolytics. Tranexamic acid reduces death due to bleeding in PPH. A: Not listed. B: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: CM-HUS.

questions.stem: Postpartum hemorrhage is defined by blood loss above what volume within 24 hours of delivery?
questions.explanation: ACOG: > 1000 mL blood loss, or blood loss with signs or symptoms of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of delivery. PPH is a leading cause of maternal death globally. B: Too low. C: Too high. D: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman has isolated thrombocytopenia with no other findings. Which cause is pregnancy-specific?
questions.explanation: Isolated thrombocytopenia: pregnancy-specific = GT; general = ITP, drug-induced, type IIB vWD, congenital. With other findings: pregnancy-specific = severe preeclampsia, HELLP, AFLP; general = TTP, CM-HUS, SLE/APS, viral, marrow, nutritional, splenic, thyroid. A: General cause. B: General cause. D: General cause. E: General cause.
